threads_text: OpenAI says its internal AI disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, an assumption hundreds of computer science papers rely on. The researchers who proposed it will now check the proof in the open, and they say that is not an endorsement. Would you trust a math proof found by an AI?
caption:
OpenAI says its internal models produced three major results: a disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a proof of the local smoothing conjecture, and existence proofs for key quantum field theories.
Outside experts, including two of the researchers who proposed ETH, will review the claims in the open.
None of the three has been independently verified yet.

Can AI really crack problems that stumped mathematicians for decades?

paragraphs.text: OpenAI said on October 26, 2026 that its internal AI models produced three major results in mathematics, theoretical computer science and physics. The headline claim is a disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, an assumption that much of complexity theory has been built on, according to The Next Web.

According to The Next Web, an OpenAI model found the disproof on October 16, and the company checked it in Lean, a language that verifies proofs by machine, the following day. The written argument and the Lean proof were posted on GitHub.
What the Exponential Time Hypothesis says

The hypothesis concerns how hard it is to solve Boolean satisfiability, a family of logic problems closely tied to the P versus NP question. Researchers use it to show that many problems in graph theory, computational biology and databases cannot be solved quickly, and hundreds of computer science papers rely on it, The Next Web reported.

Tech Insider, summarizing the technical write-up, described the result as a deterministic algorithm that counts the satisfying assignments of fixed-width formulas in subexponential time, with the 3-SAT case refuting the hypothesis. Interesting Engineering noted that refuting the hypothesis would not automatically produce faster algorithms in practice.

In mathematics, OpenAI says its models proved the local smoothing conjecture, which Christopher Sogge proposed in 1991, in every spatial dimension. The company says the proof also resolves the Kakeya conjecture and Stein's restriction conjecture. Local smoothing had previously been proved in two dimensions in 2019, and Kakeya in three dimensions in 2025, according to Interesting Engineering and The Next Web.
Tech Insider reported a possible gap in scope: OpenAI's summary says the results hold in all dimensions, while the technical description limits some of them to part of the conjectured range.

In physics, OpenAI says its models produced rigorous existence proofs for interacting quantum field theories in four dimensions, including quantum chromodynamics, and for pure Yang-Mills theory, which is tied to one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize problems. The physics materials have not been released in full.

OpenAI asked outside experts to lead independent reviews. Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of UC San Diego, who proposed the hypothesis with Francis Zane, will examine the computer science claim with Ryan Williams of MIT. The Next Web reported that the group signed no nondisclosure agreements, will not be paid, and asked OpenAI to release all raw data and fund a conference, which the company agreed to do.

The three researchers said their involvement should not be taken as certification of the claim. A physics group led by Nobel laureate David Gross, with Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov and Nikita Nekrasov, will write its own account of the physics work before the model output is released.

OpenAI says it is not seeking academic credit for the results and that the researchers who explain them should be recognized. Its previously announced $5 million contribution to the Simons Foundation will fund workshops and conferences on AI-produced results.

For now these are company claims, not accepted results. A machine-checked Lean proof shows that a formal statement follows from its premises, but experts still need to confirm that the formal statement matches the famous conjecture it is meant to settle. The decision to hand the review to the people who proposed the hypothesis gives the process unusual weight in either direction.
The next signal is the open review led by Impagliazzo, Paturi and Williams, and the release of the withheld physics materials once the Gross group finishes its write-up.
